abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii is a WHO critical-priority pathogen. Without sequencing, transmission is judged from low-resolution typing and admission records. To compare A. baumannii isolates in a Romanian county hospital by low-cost gel-based typing, test their robustness to gel sizing, and examine how admission-date sources affect the epidemiological picture. Thirteen isolates from four departments (October-December 2024) were tested by Vitek 2 and typed by multiplex PCR of eight VNTR loci on agarose gels. As bands could not be assigned to loci, band patterns were compared (Dice, UPGMA) under 25 gel-sizing assumptions. Stays reconstructed from ward records were compared with laboratory admission dates. All isolates were resistant to amikacin, ciprofloxacin, both carbapenems and tobramycin; nine (69%) were colistin-resistant by broth microdilution. One group of five isolates was separated from seven of the other eight under every sizing assumption; the eighth, and finer distinctions, were sizing-dependent. Of ten patient pairs sharing a ward, two clustered together (one with matching patterns) and seven were separated under every assumption. Laboratory admission dates lagged hospital admission in five patients. With laboratory dates the isolates formed two periods with no shared inpatient day; with reconstructed stays the periods overlapped, through one pair with matching patterns and a long-term resident whose isolate clustered with no earlier one. Some band-pattern differences persisted under every sizing assumption; whether the method can separate related from unrelated strains, and so help exclude transmission, remains to be established. Laboratory admission dates should be checked against ward-movement records.

title: Association between facility-level antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance among unexposed residents in long-term care: a population-based study
abstract: To evaluate the association between facility-level, class-specific antibiotic use and the risk of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli among long-term care residents without recent antibiotic exposure. We conducted a retrospective, population-based study of Ontario long-term care residents across 631 facilities (1 January 2017 to 31 December 2021) using a test-negative design. Eligible residents had resided 30 days or more and no systemic antibiotic exposure within 180 days before a first urine culture with E. coli or no growth. Four antibiotic-organism pairs were assessed: third-generation cephalosporin-, fluoroquinolone-, nitrofurantoin-, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)-resistant E. coli. The exposure was facility-level mean monthly use of the matched antibiotic class (days of therapy [DOT] per 1000 resident-days). Multilevel logistic regression with facility random intercepts estimated associations per 50 DOT per 1000 resident-days. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and median odds ratios (MOR) characterized between-facility variation in resistance. Of 221 007 screened urine culture events, 39 888 from non-antibiotic-exposed residents were eligible; the primary analysis included 14 907 E. coli-positive events across 620 facilities. Median resident age was 85 years (IQR 78-91) and 26 635 (67%) were female. Higher facility-level fluoroquinolone use was associated with fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli among non-exposed residents (OR 2.04; 95% CI 1.17-3.59). Associations for nitrofurantoin (OR 2.99; 95% CI 0.82-10.80), cephalosporins (OR 1.14; 95% CI 0.55-2.37), and TMP-SMX (OR 0.75; 95% CI 0.52-1.08) were not statistically significant. Residual facility variation was substantial across classes (ICC 0.02 to 0.17; MOR 1.29 to 2.21). Resident-level remote antibiotic exposure (181-365 days before index culture) was consistently associated with resistance. In residents without recent antibiotic exposure, facility-level fluoroquinolone antibiotic use was associated with antibiotic-resistant E. coli, consistent with population spillover. Antimicrobial stewardship in long-term care should address both the direct and indirect effects of antibiotic use.

title: Antimicrobial-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae in eight WHO Enhanced Gonococcal Antimicrobial Surveillance Programme sentinel countries in three WHO regions, 2021-24: a retrospective genomic surveillance study
abstract: Gonorrhoea remains a global public health concern due to increasing antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Whole-genome sequencing integrated into AMR surveillance programmes enables high-resolution tracking of Neisseria gonorrhoeae evolution and AMR spread. We describe the gonococcal population structure and AMR landscape across eight countries (Cambodia, Indonesia, Malawi, the Philippines, South Africa, Thailand, Uganda, and Viet Nam), representing three WHO regions, in the WHO Enhanced Gonococcal Antimicrobial Surveillance Programme (EGASP), 2021-24. In this retrospective genomic surveillance study, we analysed EGASP isolates (one isolate per male urethral gonorrhoea episode) collected in 2021-24 at 35 clinical sites in eight EGASP countries. Isolates underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequencing. AMR determinants and genotypes were characterised, and isolates were assigned to genomic lineages and sublineages. Phylogenomics and t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) clustering analyses were performed to evaluate transmission patterns and AMR distribution. From Nov 1, 2021, to Dec 31, 2024, 2984 EGASP isolates from Cambodia (n=474), Indonesia (n=100), Malawi (n=121), the Philippines (n=842), South Africa (n=584), Thailand (n=249), Uganda (n=367), and Viet Nam (n=247) were included. All individuals with gonorrhoea were treated in accordance with national treatment guidelines. Ceftriaxone resistance was detected in 290 (9·7%) of the 2984 isolates, all from Cambodia (224 [47%] of 474) and Viet Nam (66 [27%] of 247), and exclusively linked to the presence of penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2) A311V across 12 mosaic penA alleles. Extensive drug resistance (resistance to ceftriaxone, cefixime, azithromycin, and ciprofloxacin) was found in 72 (2·4%) of the 2984 isolates: all N gonorrhoeae sequence typing for antimicrobial resistance (NG-STAR) clonal complex (CC) 5793 and multilocus sequence typing sequence type 16406 from Cambodia. Semimosaic MtrD variants (particularly variant 13) were detected in 115 (3·9%) of the 2984 isolates, mostly associated with low-level azithromycin resistance (93 [81%] of 115) in genomic sublineages A2 and A3. Phylogenomic and t-SNE analyses revealed widely different transmission patterns at the clinical sites in 13 cities or regions in the eight WHO EGASP countries. The regional establishment of PBP2 A311V-driven ceftriaxone resistance in Cambodia and Viet Nam, along with concomitant high-level azithromycin resistance (minimum inhibitory concentration ≥256 mg/L) in Cambodia, reflects a shift from the sporadic emergence of extensively drug-resistant gonococci to stable clonal spread. Continued expansion of high-risk clones-eg, NG-STAR CC5793, threatens current treatment strategies. Expanded AMR testing, in conjunction with genomic surveillance, tailored public health responses, and accelerated development and licensing of novel treatment options such as zoliflodacin and gepotidacin, is urgently needed. WHO; Örebro University Hospital.

title: Treatment-intensity trade-offs during UV-LED/chlorine disinfection of source water: Halogenated molecular and resistome responses
abstract: UV-LED/chlorine disinfection can improve microbial control, but increasing oxidative intensity may simultaneously alter organic matter chemistry and antimicrobial-resistance-related signatures, creating a treatment trade-off that is rarely evaluated within the same water matrix. This study investigated treatment-intensity-dependent changes in solid-phase-extraction (SPE)-extractable natural organic matter, putative halogenated molecular features, and the membrane-captured resistome in source water exposed to 2-8 mg Lfree chlorine and UV fluences of 270-540 mJ cm. FT-ICR MS showed that polyphenolic and highly unsaturated phenolic formulas decreased from 75.55% to 64.45%, whereas aliphatic formulas increased from 13.36% to 24.89%, indicating oxidation and fragmentation of extractable organic matter. Assigned halogenated molecular features changed from 66 in untreated source water to 57-201 across treatments, with exact-mass-difference analysis indicating chlorine-related substitution and addition as major putative transformation pathways. Metagenomic analysis revealed a non-monotonic resistome response: recoverable total antibiotic resistance gene abundance decreased from 193.64 ×/Gb to 55.64-118.84 ×/Gb under UVCl_1-UVCl_3 (2 mg Lchlorine at 270 or 540 mJ cmand 4 mg L at 270 mJ cm), but increased to 236.98-3588.70 ×/Gb under UVCl_4-UVCl_6, accompanied by increases in efflux-related genes, mobile genetic element signatures, and putative ARG-carrying taxa. Shared halogenated molecular features co-varied with ARG profiles across treatments, but these associations were interpreted as concurrent responses to oxidative exposure rather than evidence of direct byproduct-driven regulation. Overall, increasing disinfection intensity did not produce uniformly favorable chemical and resistome outcomes, highlighting the need to optimize UV-LED/chlorine treatment by jointly considering halogenated molecular formation and antimicrobial-resistance-related responses.

title: Genomic Characterization and Protective Efficacy of a Lytic Phage Cocktail Against Vibrio anguillarum in Rainbow Trout Aquaculture
abstract: Aquaculture needs alternatives to antibiotics against vibriosis caused by Vibrio anguillarum. Three lytic bacteriophages, VP-BES, VP-ALA and VP-SUMAE, were isolated from Turkish aquaculture waters. Their genome sequences (54,898, 129,979 and 71,257 bp, respectively) lacked detectable antibiotic resistance, virulence or lysogeny genes, consistent with a lytic lifestyle; for VP-ALA and VP-SUMAE, only partial assemblies (estimated 84.2% and 76.1% complete) were screened. Intergenomic similarities of 2.4%-23.8% to their closest characterized relatives indicate three new species in two proposed new genera, one for VP-BES (≤ 0.3% to the other isolates) and one for VP-ALA and VP-SUMAE (Ackermannviridae; 70.2% mutual similarity, marginally above the 70% genus threshold). All three lysed all eight V. anguillarum strains but none of 18 non-target strains, and none was cytotoxic to EPC cells. In intraperitoneally challenged rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), 10-day survival rose significantly from 13.3% (untreated) to 86.7% with a three-phage cocktail injected intraperitoneally immediately after challenge and 73.3% with cocktail-supplemented feed from 2 days post-infection (relative percentage survival 84.6% and 69.2%). Route, timing and delivered dose differed between treatments, and tissue bacterial loads were not measured; the data therefore show protection against mortality, not route effect or bacterial clearance. These phages are promising candidates against trout vibriosis.

title: Carbonaceous materials for electrochemical pathogen detection and disease diagnosis
abstract: Pathogenic infections remain a major global health challenge, further intensified by antimicrobial resistance and the emergence of novel infectious agents. Electrochemical sensing has attracted considerable attention as a rapid, low-cost, and point-of-care approach for pathogen detection and infection monitoring. Among these sensing platforms, carbonaceous materials occupy a central role owing to their favorable electrochemical properties, including wide potential windows, facile electron-transfer kinetics, tunable surface chemistry, biocompatibility, and low-cost fabrication. This review critically examines recent advances in carbonaceous electrochemical sensors for infectious disease diagnostics, focusing on carbon films, carbon fibers, graphene and graphene derivatives, carbon nanotubes, fullerenes, graphene quantum dots, and nanodiamonds. We discuss how the structural and electronic characteristics of each material influence sensing performance, recognition element immobilization, signal transduction, and analytical figures of merit. Particular emphasis is placed on electrochemical strategies for the detection of whole pathogens, nucleic acids, proteins, and infection-associated metabolites, as well as emerging applications in continuous monitoring of microbial metabolite production, biofilm development, and antimicrobial efficacy. Carbonaceous materials enable sensitive detection across many sensor designs, but the analytical performance depends strongly on the material properties, electrode architecture, surface modification, and recognition strategy used. Translation to clinical use is limited less by sensitivity than by performance in complex samples, where biofouling, poor stability, and limited reproducibility have rarely been addressed through validation. By comparing the advantages and limitations specific to each material class, this review aims to inform the rational design of future electrochemical platforms for infectious disease diagnosis and monitoring.

title: Computational Identification of Quercetin and 6-Methoxykaempferol as Potential Sortase A Inhibitors Against Staphylococcus aureus: An Anti-Virulence Drug Discovery Approach
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is a main cause of severe infections globally, and increasing antibiotic resistance required the discovery of novel anti-virulence therapeutics. Sortase A, an enzyme involved in anchoring virulence-associated surface proteins to the bacterial cell wall, represents a crucial target for such discoveries. In this current study, library of 392 phytochemicals derived from Artemisia annua (A. annua) were screened against Sortase A by molecular docking, followed by absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity (ADMET), prediction of activity spectra for substances (PASS) analysis, 500 ns molecular dynamic (MD) simulations, and Molecular Mechanics/Poisson-Boltzmann Surface Area (MM/PBSA) analysis. Molecular docking prioritized Quercetin and 6-Methoxykaempferol which commonly shared the catalytic cavity and interacted with functionally important residues, including GLU105 and ASN114 located within the Ca²⁺ binding site. ADMET predictions exhibited favorable drug-related physiochemical and toxicological profiles, and PASS analysis predicted antibacterial and antimycobacterial activities. The 500 ns MD simulations investigated stability of protein-ligand complexes, with Quercetin exhibited comparatively lower structural fluctuations, whereas 6-Methoxykaempferol displayed greater conformational flexibility. Principal component and free energy landscape analyses further characterized the conformational behavior of both complexes. MM/PBSA analysis exhibited favorable estimated binding free energies of -8.53 ± 6.83 for Quercetin and - 13.45 ± 2.57 kcal/mol for 6-Methoxykaempferol. However, this study has limitations including chemical diversity of the available phytochemical database and the predictive nature of docking, ADMET, PASS, and dynamics analyses which require experimental validation. Overall, these findings identify Quercetin and 6-Methoxykaempferol as computationally promising phytochemical candidates for further development as Sortase A inhibitors.

title: Sustainable Removal of Ciprofloxacin from Aqueous Media Using Pine Needle Biosorbent
abstract: The increasing use of antibiotics and the inadequacy of conventional treatment systems contribute to their accumulation and the spread of antibiotic resistance in aquatic environments, posing significant environmental and public health concerns. In this study, the removal of ciprofloxacin from aqueous solutions by adsorption was investigated using a low-cost and environmentally friendly biosorbent derived from pine needles. The biosorbent was prepared using a water-based modification method and characterized in terms of surface morphology, specific surface area, and pore properties. The effects of operational parameters, including solution pH, adsorbent dose, initial ciprofloxacin concentration, and contact time, on biosorption performance were investigated. Despite its low specific surface area (1.13 m²/g) and macroporous structure, the biosorbent exhibited high removal efficiency. The pH at the point of zero charge (pHpzc) was determined to be 4.77. Considering the amphoteric nature of ciprofloxacin and the surface charge of the adsorbent, electrostatic interactions, as well as hydrogen bonding and π-π interactions, are considered to contribute to adsorption under neutral and slightly acidic conditions. High removal efficiency (> 90%) was achieved under the optimum conditions of pH 7, an initial ciprofloxacin concentration of 30 mg/L, a contact time of 90 min, and an adsorbent dosage of 100 mg/50 mL. Kinetic analyses indicated that the adsorption process followed a pseudo-second-order model, while equilibrium data were best described by the Langmuir isotherm, yielding a maximum adsorption capacity of approximately 47.6 mg/g. Thermodynamic analysis indicated that the adsorption process was spontaneous and exothermic and was predominantly governed by physical interactions. These findings demonstrate that pine needle-derived biosorbents represent a sustainable and economical alternative for antibiotic removal from aqueous media.

title: Sputum bacteria and antibiotic resistance in adults hospitalised with asthma: a 27-year longitudinal analysis
Selenium formulation shapes antibiotic resistome across a soil-radish continuum
abstract: Selenium biofortification is widely used to improve crop Se content, but the effects of different Se formulations on antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in organic fertilizer-amended agricultural systems remain unclear. Here, we compared dissolved selenite (Se), chemically synthesized nano-selenium (CNSe), and biologically synthesized nano-selenium (BNSe) at an equivalent dose (0.5 mg kg) in a cherry radish pot experiment, and characterized resistomes in soil and radish tissues using high-throughput qPCR. Se formulations did not significantly alter total ARG relative abundance in either habitat, but they restructured ARG composition in both soil and radish. Partitioning β-diversity showed that compositional dissimilarity was primarily driven by subtype turnover rather than nestedness, and null-model analysis indicated that stochastic processes dominated resistome assembly. Shared ARG accounted for more than 99% of the ARG abundance in radish, while Se formulation altered abundance-based ARG similarity across the soil-radish continuum. Together, these findings show that Se formulation shapes resistome composition and distribution in soil-radish continuum, providing experimental evidence for assessing the microbiological implications of Se-based biofortification.

title: Quorum sensing enhances simultaneous nitrogen and phosphorus removal and oxidative stress adaptation in heterotrophic nitrification-aerobic denitrification bacterium Alcaligenes sp. J8 under oxytetracycline exposure
abstract: Quorum sensing (QS) plays a crucial role in regulating microbial metabolism. However, its role in heterotrophic nitrification-aerobic denitrification (HN-AD) bacteria's response to antibiotic stress remains unclear. In this study, an HN-AD bacterium, Alcaligenes sp. J8, was isolated from chicken manure. It exhibited effective nitrogen and phosphorus removal and oxytetracycline (OTC) biotransformation under OTC exposure concentrations ranging from 0 to 100 mg/L. 3-oxo-C12-homoserine lactone (3OC12-HSL) was predominant in the QS system, reaching a maximum concentration of 348.4 ng/L under 50 mg/L OTC exposure. Enhancing quorum sensing can effectively improve the nitrogen and phosphorus removal performance and alleviate OTC-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. Exogenous addition of 3OC12-HSL increased the maximum nitrogen removal rate from 4.13 to 4.31 mg/(L·h), and the PO-P removal efficiency at t = 24 h increased from 63.6% in the control group to 76.6%. ROS generated under low-concentration OTC stress can act as a second messenger to activate the QS system and induce N-acyl homoserine lactone release. Transcriptomic and quantitative real-time PCR analyses revealed that QS enhanced the antibiotic resistance of strain J8 and helped it cope with antibiotic stress by adjusting nitrogen metabolism pathways and upregulating the expression of efflux pump system operon genes, namely MexAB-OprM, Mexxy-OprM, and MexGHI-OpmD. This study demonstrates that QS regulation can enhance the nitrogen and phosphorus removal capacity of HN-AD bacteria under antibiotic stress, providing an alternative strategy for treating livestock and poultry wastewater containing antibiotic residues.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance in Ukraine and Neighboring Poland Before and During Russia's Full-Scale Invasion of Ukraine: A Comparative Analysis of Public Surveillance Data, 2019-2025
abstract: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 brought war injuries, overcrowded hospitals and transfers of patients across borders, all of which favor the spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). National trends before and during the war have not been compared with those of a neighboring country. This retrospective study used publicly available, aggregated surveillance data on invasive isolates from the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Europe for Ukraine (2019-2023) and from the European Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network for Poland (2019-2025). Five pathogen-antibiotic combinations were compared between the pre-war (2019-2021) and war (2022-2023) periods using risk ratios (RR), a test for trend and a difference-in-differences analysis. Carbapenem resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae rose from 61.0% to 71.3% in Ukraine (RR 1.17, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.07-1.27) and from 12.5% to 17.5% in Poland (RR 1.41, 95% CI: 1.25-1.58). In Poland, most of the increase occurred in 2021, before the invasion. Carbapenem resistance in Acinetobacter species increased in Ukraine (74.2% to 83.0%) but not in Poland (79.1% to 78.1%; ratio of odds ratios 1.80, 95% CI: 1.17-2.77). Meanwhile, Ukrainian surveillance coverage increased from 1% to 45% of the population, and blood culture rates remained low. Reported carbapenem resistance in Ukraine was very high before the full-scale war and higher during it, most clearly in Acinetobacter species. Because surveillance expanded and the COVID-19 pandemic and antibiotic use also changed over this period, these data cannot show that the war caused the increase. Stronger infection control and coordinated cross-border surveillance are needed.

title: Multi-media distribution and ecological risk of antibiotics and antibiotic resistance genes at a State-controlled section of the Yangtze River Estuary
abstract: This study presented a comprehensive assessment of antibiotic contamination dynamics at the XuLiujing (XuLJ) Section, a critical state-controlled section of the Yangtze River Estuary. From October 2023 to November 2024, 15 antibiotics across four classes (fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, macrolides), antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), microbial communities, and pollutant fluxes in water and sediment phases were investigated. While overall water quality met Class I/II standards, antibiotics were ubiquitously detected. Sulfonamides (SAs; e.g., sulfamethoxazole up to 36.74 ng/L) and fluoroquinolones (FQs; e.g., ciprofloxacin up to 57.28 ng/L) dominated the water phase, whereas FQs and tetracyclines prevailed in sediments. ARGs sul1 and sul2 exhibited near 100% detection frequency in both phases, with tetX abundance correlating significantly with nutrients (TN, NH-N) and specific antibiotics (P < 0.05). Redundancy analysis identified the intI as a key driver for ARG dissemination. Antibiotic flux to the sea peaked at 0.65 t/month (May 2024), driven by compound-specific concentrations rather than runoff volume alone-notably, high-flow periods reduced fluxes via dilution. Proteobacteria dominated microbial communities in both water and sedimentary phases, and its abundance was linked to the nitrogen and phosphorus cycle. Antibiotic exposure significantly altered the phylum-level community structure. Ecological risk assessment revealed consistently high risk to algae from ciprofloxacin and sulfamethoxazole (RQ > 1), moderate risk to invertebrates from quinolones, and low human health risk (HQ < 0.1) via drinking water. These findings elucidate the multi-media interactions of antibiotics in estuarine systems and provide a scientific basis for ecological risk management in the Yangtze River Basin.

title: Optimization and Characterization of Vibrio-Derived Postbiotic Against Vibrio alginolyticus and Vibrio parahaemolyticus
abstract: Vibriosis is a major infectious disease affecting aquaculture, caused by Vibrio species such as Vibrio alginolyticus (VA) and Vibrio parahaemolyticus (VP), with widespread antibiotic resistance (AMR) in Vibrio spp. Postbiotics, primarily composed of fatty acids and bacteriocins, offer a sustainable alternative. This study aimed to optimize culture conditions for Vibrio-derived postbiotics rather than from lactic acid bacteria with targeted anti-Vibrio activity and identify their active components. Central Composite Design (CCD) was applied to optimize postbiotic production by manipulating candidate species (VA or VP), temperature (25-45 °C) and salinity (1.5-9.0%). Cell-free supernatants (CFS) were prepared, and anti-Vibrio activity was assessed. Fatty acid, bacteriocin-like inhibitory substance, and hydrogen peroxide-dependent activity were evaluated via pH adjustment, protease, and catalase treatments, respectively. Organic acids and fatty acids were extracted with ethyl acetate and analyzed using GC-MS, while MIC assays confirmed antibacterial activity. Optimal postbiotic production was achieved using VA at 36 °C and 1.5% salinity, yielding CFS that inhibited VA growth by 23.3%. Fatty acid-dependent inhibition contributed 18%, hydrogen peroxide ~ 7.8%, while bacteriocin-like activity was negligible (~ 1.4%). GC-MS identified oleic acid (40%) and tridecanoic acid (25%) as the major components. Both compounds exhibited moderate antibacterial activity with MICs of 500 µg/mL against VA and VP. CCD successfully optimized Vibrio postbiotic production, yielding oleic acid and tridecanoic acid as the major components. These Vibrio-derived postbiotics show potential as targeted, eco-friendly alternatives to antibiotics for sustainable vibriosis management and AMR mitigation in aquaculture.

title: Combinatorial Synthesis and Direct-to-Biology Antibacterial Evaluation of Ruthenium(II) and Iridium(III) N^O-Schiff-Base Complexes
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a major global health challenge, compounded by a limited antibiotic discovery pipeline and restricted chemical diversity among clinically used antibiotics. Metal-based complexes offer promising antimicrobial agents owing to their structural diversity and unique modes of action. Here, we report the synthesis and biological evaluation of two combinatorial libraries comprising 176 novel ruthenium(II) p-cymene (RuCy) and iridium(III) Cp* (IrCp) N^O-Schiff-base complexes. Syntheses used a robust three-step, room-temperature methodology, with automated LC-MS characterization enabling Direct-to-Biology screening. Against Staphylococcus aureus, 50-80% of compounds inhibited growth, whereas no significant activity was observed against Escherichia coli. Three leads exhibited MICs of 1.56-12.5 μM against Gram-positive pathogens, therapeutic indices exceeding 15, and negligible haemolysis. Mechanistic studies suggest that IrCp-B5, incorporating the ligand (E)-2-bromo-4-chloro-6-(((naphthalen-2-ylmethyl)imino)methyl)phenol, disrupts membrane associated processes, while RuCy-J3, incorporating (E)-1-((cyclohexylimino)methyl)naphthalen-2-ol, targets intracellular DNA-related pathways. This work demonstrates the utility of Direct-to-Biology approaches for accelerated antimicrobial lead identification and prioritization.

title: Discovery of Ebselen Analogs as Novel Inhibitors of Polyphosphate Metabolism to Attenuate Virulence and Show Combination Benefit with Meropenem in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major opportunistic pathogen responsible for severe hospital-acquired infections. The challenge in treating these infections is exacerbated by increasing antibiotic resistance. Polyphosphate kinases (PPKs), specifically PPK1 and PPK2, play a critical role in the virulence, stress response, and antibiotic tolerance of P. aeruginosa, making it a compelling target for therapeutic intervention. In this study, we describe the discovery and development of ebselen analogs as novel inhibitors against PPK1Pa and PPK2Pa. Biochemical and cellular assays revealed that ebselens interfere with the polyphosphate homeostasis within the bacterium. EB-1 and EB-18 treatment significantly reduced intracellular polyP levels, mirroring the phenotypic effects observed in Δppk strains, including impaired biofilm formation, reduced motility, and attenuated production of pyoverdine and pyocyanin. Notably, EB-1 and EB-18 showed combination benefit with meropenem against P. aeruginosa in the Galleria model, supporting their potential as an adjunctive agent to improve the antibacterial efficacy of meropenem. Most representative compounds, including EB-1 and EB-18, showed no detectable cytotoxicity in the tested mammalian cells. These findings underscore ebselen analogs as promising dual-specific PPK inhibitors, establishing a valuable strategy for the development of adjunct therapies via the PPK-mediated anti-virulence pathways.

title: Profiling antibiotic resistance genes, virulence factors, and carbohydrate-active enzymes using metagenomics: implications for Plateau Wetland ecological health
abstract: This study employs metagenomic analysis to systematically characterize the diversity and abundance of CAZymes, ARGs, and VFs in water and soil samples collected from the Napahai Plateau Wetland. Significant differences in α-diversity were observed across the sample types, with VFs exhibiting the most pronounced variation. PCoA revealed distinct clustering of water and soil samples based on the abundance profiles of ARGs and VFs, whereas CAZymes displayed relatively uniform distribution across both environments. Among CAZymes, GH and GT were the most prevalent, with PL and AA enriched in water, and CBM and GH more abundant in soil. ARGs associated with aminoglycoside and sulfonamide resistance were more prevalent in water, whereas soil samples exhibited a higher abundance of genes such as acrR and vanI. Additionally, VFs related to exotoxins and motility were significantly more abundant in aquatic environments, indicating a potentially heightened pathogenic potential in these settings. Environmental variables, including pH, TN, TP, and metal ions (Zn, Mg), were significantly correlated with CAZymes and VFs abundance. For ARGs, these correlations are likely indirect and mediated by shifts in microbial community composition and abundance. Notably, a positive correlation among CAZymes, ARGs, and VFs suggested their co-enrichment, likely driven by microbial adaptation to ecological stressors such as antibiotic pollution. These findings highlight the critical role of plateau wetlands as reservoirs and potential dissemination hubs for antibiotic resistance and microbial virulence, with important implications for ecosystem health and public health surveillance amidst global environmental change.

title: Pericardial abscess caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa with emergence of carbapenem resistance during treatment: A case report
abstract: A 51-year-old immunocompromised woman was incidentally found to have purulent pericarditis caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa following a traumatic injury. Initial treatment with pericardial drainage, surgical pericardiotomy, and systemic antibiotic therapy with meropenem led to clinical improvement. However, the pericardial abscess subsequently recurred, and the recurrent isolate had acquired meropenem resistance. Whole-genome sequencing of isolates obtained at initial drainage and at recurrence identified an oprD nonsense mutation (p.Trp277*) detected exclusively in the recurrent isolate, providing a plausible mechanism for the emergence of carbapenem resistance. The patient was successfully treated with repeat drainage and ceftolozane/tazobactam, without further recurrence. Purulent pericarditis caused by P. aeruginosa is exceedingly rare, and genomic analysis can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying acquired antimicrobial resistance.

title: Bacterial neonatal conjunctivitis in a neonatal intensive care unit: incidence, aetiology, predictors, and antimicrobial resistance
Antibiotic use in canine breeding: What German-speaking breeders do, think and expect
abstract: The canine vagina harbours a diverse and dynamic microbiome and the detection of bacteria in clinically healthy bitches does not in itself indicate infection. Nevertheless, bacteriological examination prior to mating and subsequent antibiotic treatment are widely applied in dog breeding. While veterinarians' practices in this field have recently been described, comparatively little is known about breeders' perspectives in Germany. The aim of this study was to provide an up-to-date overview of the pre-mating veterinary examinations, antibiotics use, knowledge about the vaginal microbiota and beliefs of breeders in German-speaking countries, to better target educational efforts. An online questionnaire comprising 49 questions was distributed from September 2025 to December 2025. The survey evaluation included 834 breeders, mainly from Germany. Responses were analysed descriptively and via multiple logistic regression, chi-squared test and Fisher's exact test to identify factors associated with breeders' responses. Vaginal swabs were arranged before every mating by 46% of respondents, and sampling was initiated by the breeders themselves in 90% of cases. Antibiotics had never been administered before mating according to 56% of the respondents, whereas 36% reported occasional, 6% regular and 2% routine use, with differing frequency depending on the type of breed. The most frequently given reason was a veterinary recommendation based on bacteria detected in a vaginal swab (79%) in close collaboration with the veterinarian, although 92% stated they would not administer antibiotics prophylactically without a clear medical indication. Uncertainty was pronounced, as 48% were unable to judge which bacteria might impair mating outcome. Of the remaining respondents who did identify specific bacteria, Mycoplasma spp. was selected most frequently (36%). In contrast, 75% identified incorrect timing of mating as the most common cause for conception failure. A total of 87% reported familiarity with antimicrobial resistance. Bacteriological screening and situation-dependent antibiotic use thus remain common in clinically healthy bitches despite limited evidence supporting their use. Although awareness of resistance is high and veterinarians are widely trusted, misconceptions regarding the clinical relevance of bacterial findings appear to persist, underlining the need for evidence-based education of breeders, veterinarians and kennel clubs, and clear recommendations on whether and when to treat clinically healthy breeding bitches.

title: Microwave-assisted synthesis of thioether-linked sulfonamides as dual DHPS/DHFR inhibitors: biological evaluation and molecular dynamics studies
abstract: The increasing burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) highlights the need for structurally diverse antibacterial agents targeting established bacterial pathways. Sulfonamides and diaminopyrimidines inhibit successive enzymes in bacterial folate biosynthesis, dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) and dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), respectively. The emergence of resistant bacterial strains motivates the development of molecular frameworks capable of inhibiting both enzymes. This study investigated the molecular hybridisation of sulfonamide and thiol-containing heterocyclic pharmacophores to develop antibacterial candidates with potential dual DHPS/DHFR inhibitory activity. Eight thioether-linked sulfonamide derivatives (4a-d and 6a-d) were synthesised using microwave-assisted heating, achieving 92-95% yields within 7-10 min. Antibacterial evaluation against Gram-positive and Gram-negative strains, including clinical methicillin-resistant(MRSA), identified compound 4a as the most active derivative against MRSA (MIC = 2 µg mL). Enzyme inhibition assays confirmed inhibitory activity against both DHPS and DHFR for compounds 4a and 6a. Compound 4a exhibited ICvalues of 0.6464 and 0.4196 µg mLagainst DHPS and DHFR, respectively, compared with 1.4815 and 0.8415 µg mLfor compound 6a. Molecular docking, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations, MM-GBSA, and conformational analyses provided insights into the interactions and dynamics of the 4a-DHPS and 4a-DHFR complexes. Compound 4a additionally demonstrated DPPH radical-scavenging activity comparable to ascorbic acid, limited cytotoxicity under tested conditions, and DNA association without pronounced cleavage. ADMET predictions provided preliminary pharmacokinetic and toxicity insights. Taken together, these results identify compound 4a as a promising antibacterial lead with inhibitory activity against both DHPS and DHFR, supporting its further investigation.

title: An efficient hypoxia-tolerant photosensitizer targeting arginine metabolism for combating drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in diabetic foot infection
abstract: Diabetic foot infection (DFI) is characterized by robust biofilm formation and pronounced antibiotic resistance in(), leading to high amputation and mortality rates and necessitating alternative anti-infective strategies. A hypoxia-tolerant photosensitizer, QTAE nanoparticles (NPs), is developed for photodynamic treatment of DFI. QTAE NPs exhibit favorable photophysical properties and efficiently generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) and singlet oxygen under light irradiation. Potent antibacterial activity is observed againstATCC 25923 and methicillin-resistant(MRSA), without detectable resistance after 40 consecutive passages. Mechanistically, QTAE NPs inhibit bacterial growth and biofilm formation by downregulating, a key gene in the arginine catabolic mobile element pathway, thereby disrupting arginine metabolism in MRSA. In diabetic mouse models, QTAE NPs effectively eradicate MRSA infection and accelerate wound healing, accompanied by macrophage polarization from M1 to M2, reduced inflammation and oxidative stress, and increased Ki-67 expression, without observable toxicity to major organs. QTAE NPs thus represent a promising hypoxia-tolerant photodynamic platform for treating drug-resistant DFI.

title: Sources and drivers of antibiotic resistance genes across rivers and lakes
abstract: River and lake ecosystems are important reservoirs and transmission pathways for antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), yet the global distribution, sources and risks of their resistomes remain poorly understood. Here we analysed 4,128 river and lake metagenomes (water and sediment) from 42 countries and regions and constructed a comprehensive genome-resolved catalogue of ARG-carrying bacteria, revealing key pathogenic vectors of resistance. Clinically important ARGs, including blaand mcr, were widespread and showed distinct biogeographical patterns, highlighting rivers and lakes as potential sentinels for global antimicrobial resistance surveillance. Here, using an integrative source-tracking framework, we identified aquaculture, hospital sewage and municipal sewage as major contributors to riverine resistomes, with the estimated contribution of aquaculture increasing from 11% in 2012 to 40% in 2020. Human population and aquaculture intensity emerged as key drivers of the distribution and associated risks of river and lake resistomes. We further generated a predictive global map of freshwater resistome risk. By transforming metagenomic data into a tool for tracing antimicrobial resistance, our study establishes rivers as potential early-warning systems and supports their integration into One Health surveillance frameworks.

title: Preliminary In Vivo Evaluation of a Periodontal Biogel Incorporating Mānuka Oil-Loaded Chitosan Nanoparticles
abstract: Current periodontal treatment focuses on dental biofilm removal, with adjunctive antimicrobial therapy. Concerns about antibiotic resistance have increased interest in natural antimicrobial agents. This study investigated the sterilization and preliminary in vivo effects of a carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) biogel incorporating mānuka oil and β-triketone-loaded chitosan nanoparticles using a ligature-induced rat periodontitis model. Formulations were sterilized by gamma irradiation or UV exposure. In vivo outcomes were assessed by micro-computed tomography (micro-CT), histological staining, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) staining, CD45 immunohistochemistry, and 16S rRNA sequencing. UV irradiation effectively sterilized the composites without changing oil composition, nanoparticle structure, or gel syringeability. The mānuka oil-loaded nanoparticle-gel showed lower CEJ-alveolar bone than the commercial CURAPROX control. Histological assessment showed no severe inflammatory response across the groups, while qualitative TRAP staining showed no TRAP-positive cells along the bone surface in the mānuka oil group, with only a few positive cells observed within the bone. CD45-positive cells were primarily restricted to the superficial gingival tissue. Microbiome analysis revealed changes in microbial composition across treatment groups. These findings provide preliminary information on the in vivo biological performance of a CMC biogel incorporating mānuka oil nanoparticles, supporting further investigation to determine its potential application in periodontal therapy.

title: Causal effects of extreme climate hazards on antimicrobial resistance across One Health reservoirs: protocol for a scoping review and evidence gap map
abstract: Extreme climate events are increasing in frequency and intensity, with potential consequences for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) across One Health reservoirs. However, the evidence base remains fragmented, and the capacity of existing studies to support causal inference has not been systematically assessed. This scoping review aims to map evidence linking extreme climate hazards to AMR outcomes across human, animal and environmental reservoirs; assess causal inference potential of identified studies and identify critical evidence gaps. 10 bibliographic databases are being searched for studies published from January 2000 to August 2026, with final updates and supplementary searches planned for November 2026. Searches began in December 2025; screening of records retrieved to date is complete, but data extraction and causal inference assessment have not started. Two reviewers (CH and TPN), with SL adjudicating disagreements, will independently extract data and assess studies of six extreme climate hazard categories across human, animal and environmental reservoirs. An eight-criterion causal inference potential framework will provide criterion profiles and descriptive scores from 0 to 16; its unvalidated weighting and classification thresholds will be examined in sensitivity analyses. Inter-rater agreement will be reported before consensus. A 6×8 evidence gap map will summarise study coverage, with separate sub-reservoir and outcome domain displays for antimicrobial use, phenotypic resistance and genotypic resistance. Harvest plots and narrative synthesis will preserve these distinctions. The review is expected to be completed in February 2027. This scoping review will analyse existing published data; therefore, ethical approval is not required. The completed review will be submitted for publication in a peer-reviewed open access journal. The evidence gap map, harvest plots and underlying dataset will be made publicly available through an open data repository. Findings will be disseminated through scientific conferences and briefing materials for relevant international initiatives.

title: River Recreational Swimming: A Non-negligible Source of Aquatic Antibiotic Resistance Genes and Pathogenic Bacteria
abstract: Water-based recreational activities represent an important pathway for introducing microbial contaminants into aquatic systems. However, the impact of river swimming on riverine antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and human bacterial pathogens (HBPs, including potential HBPs) remains poorly characterized. In this study, we investigated the longitudinal variations of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), mobile genetic elements (MGEs), and HBPs in three river swimming zones with different human traffic densities. The results showed a significant increase in the cumulative absolute abundance of ARGs (0.20 to 1.01 logunits) after swimming activities, which was positively associated with swimmer traffic. Taxonomic profiling based on full-length 16S rRNA sequencing also revealed that swimming activities could drive a 2.24-to-2.78-fold enrichment of potential HBPs in proximal downstream water. Longitudinal tracking of the river with the highest swimmer traffic showed a natural attenuation of ARGs and shared HBPs in distal downstream water, indicating the self-purification capacity of river systems, but their abundance remained higher than upstream baseline levels. Network analysis further exhibited significant co-occurrence patterns among potential HBPs, ARGs, and MGEs, suggesting possible ARG carriage by HBPs and a theoretical risk of MGE-facilitated dissemination in river water. Finally, SourceTracker analysis revealed that skin and saliva were important contributors to the proximal downstream microbial load. This study provides comprehensive insights into swimming-induced microbial pollution and highlights the urgent need for implementing source controls to safeguard public health in recreational rivers.

title: Species-Specific Shifts in Bloodstream Infection Epidemiology and Antimicrobial Resistance in Patients With Hematologic Malignancies: A Six-Year Study
abstract: To characterize six-year species-specific changes in bloodstream infection (BSI) incidence in patients with hematologic malignancies and describe documented antimicrobial resistance phenotypes. We retrospectively analyzed microbiologically documented BSI episodes from 2020-2025 using annual patient-days as the exposure denominator. Temporal trends were estimated by Poisson regression. Generalized estimating equations assessed pathogen representation while accounting for recurrent BSI and selected case-mix characteristics. A total of 203 BSI episodes occurred in 101 patients over 71,404 patient-days. Overall BSI incidence increased over time (IRR per year 1.237, 95% CI 1.027-1.490; p = 0.0249). Klebsiella pneumoniae incidence increased markedly (IRR 2.036, 95% CI 1.411-2.940; p < 0.001), as did Enterococcus faecium incidence (IRR 1.568, 95% CI 1.13-2.17; p = 0.0066). The vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) incidence trend was not statistically significant (IRR 1.49, 95% CI 0.86-2.58; p = 0.156). BSI burden increased over six years, with a marked species-specific expansion of K. pneumoniae. Species-specific longitudinal surveillance may reveal changes obscured by aggregate BSI counts.

title: Incidence of Mycoplasma genitalium infection and prevalence of antimicrobial resistance markers in men who have sex with men receiving doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis in France: a secondary outcome analysis of the ANRS 174 DOXYVAC randomised trial
abstract: Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (DoxyPEP) reduces bacterial sexually transmitted infections among men who have sex with men (MSM), but its effect on Mycoplasma genitalium infection and potential to select for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remain uncertain. We assessed M genitalium incidence in MSM and the effect of DoxyPEP on markers associated with M genitalium AMR in a secondary analysis of the ANRS 174 DOXYVAC trial. In this open-label, 2 × 2 factorial randomised trial at ten hospital sites in Paris, MSM receiving HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis and with a bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the previous year were assigned (2:1) to receive doxycycline 200 mg orally within 72 h after condomless sex (up to three doses weekly) or no PEP, independently of meningococcal group B vaccination. Anal, urine, and throat samples underwent M genitalium PCR at baseline and every 3 months. Mutations in 23S rRNA, 16S rRNA, parC, and gyrA were assessed in positive samples (cycle threshold ≤30); mgpB sequencing was used for typing. Cox regression adjusted for vaccination estimated the first-infection hazard ratio; Fisher's exact tests compared resistance markers and sequence types. Analyses included participants with at least one follow-up visit. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04597424). Recruitment is complete. Between Jan 19, 2021, and Sept 19, 2022, 545 participants (median age 40 years [IQR 34-49]) were assigned to receive DoxyPEP (n=362) or no PEP (n=183). At baseline, 481 (88%) of 545 participants were recorded as White, 13 (2%) as Black, 13 (2%) as Asian, and 38 (7%) as other or unknown ethnicity. Overall, 138 (25%) of 545 participants had M genitalium infection. The incidence of a first M genitalium infection was 32·3 per 100 person-years (114 events) in the DoxyPEP group versus 44·9 (73 events) in the no-PEP group (adjusted hazard ratio 0·72 [95% CI 0·54-0·96]; p=0·027). During follow-up, macrolide resistance-associated mutations were detected in 26 (76%) of 34 samples in the DoxyPEP group versus 32 (94%) of 34 in the no-PEP group (p=0·083); fluoroquinolone resistance-associated mutations in 19 (54%) of 35 versus 17 (53%) of 32 (p>0·99); and 16S rRNA tetracycline-binding-site mutations in two (6%) of 32 versus six (22%) of 27 (p=0·13). Among 133 M genitalium-positive samples, 28 mgpB sequence types were identified, with no significant difference in distribution between groups (p=0·91). Dual-resistant ST159 was most frequent (43 [32%] of 133 samples). DoxyPEP modestly reduced M genitalium incidence among MSM receiving HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis without a detected increase in resistance-associated mutations or selection of dual-resistant ST159, although limited testing constrains interpretation. These findings are consistent with guidance to restrict M genitalium testing and treatment to patients with symptomatic infections and highlight the need for AMR surveillance as DoxyPEP use expands. title: Synergistic antimicrobial and antibiofilm activity of hydroethanolic extracts of Cinnamomum verum J. Presl and Punica granatum L. against multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Antibiotic resistance in pathogens, such as Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, represents a global health threat, highlighting the need for therapeutic alternatives. Investigate the synergistic antimicrobial and antibiofilm potential of Cinnamomum verum and Punica granatum extracts against multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains of A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa, along with their phytochemical composition and antioxidant activity. The extracts were characterized by total phenolic and flavonoid contents, and their bioactive compounds were identified using HPLC. Antioxidant activity was evaluated by free-radical scavenging assays. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) were determined by microdilution method. Synergistic interactions between the extracts were assessed by the checkerboard microdilution assay. The antibiofilm activity of the extracts was evaluated by their ability to inhibit biofilm formation and to reduce preformed biofilms of MDR strains. Both extracts exhibited antioxidant activity and antibacterial effects, with minimum bactericidal concentrations as low as 3.3 mg/mL. C. verum showed 0.935 mg/mL of flavonoids and 2.069 mg/mL of phenolics, while P. granatum showed 0.853 mg/mL and 1.406 mg/mL, respectively. The combination of extracts showed synergistic antimicrobial interactions, with 12 synergistic combinations (FIC ≤ 0.5), particularly against A. baumannii. Concentrations of C. verum and P. granatum extracts inhibited biofilm formation in A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa, with effects comparable to chlorhexidine. Extracts of C. verum and P. granatum exhibit relevant antimicrobial and antibiofilm activities, with synergistic interactions. Their combination represents a promising natural strategy to enhance antimicrobial efficacy against MDR pathogens.

title: Rapid Molecular Diagnostics and the "Cost of Wait": An Expert Opinion on Clinical Excellence and Economic Sustainability in the Era of Rising Antimicrobial Resistance
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was associated with an estimated 4.71 million deaths in 2021, and direct healthcare costs attributable to AMR are projected to reach US$159 billion/year by 2050. Reliance on culture-based diagnostics, which require 48-72 h for pathogen identification and susceptibility testing, contributes to a "cost of wait", characterized by prolonged empirical broad-spectrum therapy and potentially worse outcomes. This expert opinion is based on four interactive in-person sessions of the 6th Middle East, North Africa, and Commonwealth of Independent States (MENA/CIS) Xpert Champions' Club (2025), in which infectious disease specialists, clinical microbiologists, and health economists from six Gulf Cooperation Council countries discussed the clinical, economic, and policy role of rapid molecular diagnostics (RMD), with emphasis on the Gulf region. Session transcripts were analyzed thematically, and the panel's perspectives were contextualized with literature identified through a targeted search. The panel considered the integration of RMD with antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) a clinical priority. Meta-analyses in bloodstream infection suggest that this combination is associated with lower mortality and shorter time to optimal therapy, whereas RMD without stewardship show little survival benefit. Economic evaluations, largely model-based and conducted outside the region, suggest that RMD combined with ASPs is likely to be cost-effective, although results depend on test volume and setting. RMD complement rather than replace culture and phenotypic susceptibility testing and are limited by panel coverage, specimen quality, and the inability to distinguish colonization from infection. The panel identified settings in which RMD are most likely to add value: time-critical inpatient care, admission screening for multidrug-resistant organisms, intrapartum testing of women with unknown group B Streptococcus (GBS) status, and initial testing for tuberculosis (TB), within a One Health policy framework. When targeted to appropriate settings and embedded in stewardship, RMD may improve clinical outcomes and support value-based healthcare in the Gulf region. Region-specific studies of clinical impact and cost-effectiveness are needed.

title: Klebsiella pneumoniae ST268 in Saffron Finches Seized from an Illegal Bird Fighting: Linking Antimicrobial Resistance, Environmental Violations, and Animal Welfare
abstract: Illegal wildlife trade (IWT) is often associated with the neglect of sanitary protocols, and proper animal handling, which may play a significant role in the evolution of bacteria harboring antimicrobial resistance mechanisms. The present study aimed to detect enteropathogens of global public health concern colonizing saffron finches (Sicalis flaveola) recovered from an illegal bird fighting activity. A total of 101 fecal samples were collected from saffron finches, from which 96 bacterial isolates were recovered and characterized. The Escherichia coli and Klebsiella spp. isolates were submitted to antimicrobial susceptibility testing (n = 61), and among them, only those belonging to the Klebsiella pneumoniae complex (n = 44) showed antimicrobial resistance (13/44; 29.5%). Nine Klebsiella pneumoniae complex was identified as extended-spectrum β-lactamase producers, and four displayed the hypermucoviscous phenotype. Four isolates of interest were sequenced based on phenotypic and molecular evidence of ESBL production, antimicrobial resistance profiles, the hypermucoviscous phenotype, given its potential association with hypervirulence in K. pneumoniae; and the saffron finch subspecies from which each isolate was obtained. Whole-genome sequencing revealed two lineages (ST268-KL20 and ST1876-KL127) carrying the pandemic variant bla. The ST268 K. pneumoniae strains displayed the hypermucoviscous phenotype, despite the absence of genes associated with this phenotype, such as the rmpA/A2. These findings were observed in individuals from both endemic and exotic subspecies of S. flaveola sampled in the study, and have previously been reported in human, domestic animals, and environmental samples. Finally, this is the first known report of ST268 and ST1876 clones colonizing wild birds. Conditions associated with IWT and bird fighting may be linked to the emergence of multidrug-resistant lineages in these birds, revealing the need for antimicrobial resistance surveillance strategies across One Health sector. Furthermore, the detection of epidemiologically relevant bacterial clones already reported in other regions of the world reinforces the multifactorial nature of AMR and highlights the role of IWT in its global potential dissemination.

From microbial processes to human inhalation health risk: genome-informed quantitative assessment of atmospheric pathogens during haze and dust events
abstract: Although haze and dust events alter atmospheric microbial composition and pathogenic genetic traits, their differential implications for inhalation exposure remain poorly understood, with frameworks to translate genomic divergence into human infection risk predictions especially lacking. Integrating metagenomics, neutral modeling, metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) binning, comparative genomics, and quantitative microbial risk assessment (QMRA), we deciphered community ecology, genetic co-localization, and health risks of bioaerosols during autumn-winter haze and spring dust events in Xi'an, China. Results revealed contrasting ecological patterns: spring dust featured greater microbial dispersal, broader niches, and more stress-survival-associated virulence factors (VFs), with terrestrial inputs indicated by desert-associated Geodermatophilus obscurus (2.5%), whereas autumn-winter haze featured local microbial accumulation, with abundant Escherichia coli (32.6%) and Klebsiella aerogenes (18.6%). Co-occurrence networks revealed 2,054 cross-component associations among pathogens, antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), mobile genetic elements (MGEs), and VFs, while genome-resolved analysis identified 10 ARG-MGE and 230 VF-MGE proximity records across 16 MAGs. Neutral modeling showed better fits for risk-related functional components than for microbial taxa, with greater stochasticity during spring dust. For risk modeling, comparative genomics of 13 Enterobacteriaceae strains identified adhesin gene density as a potential genomic predictor of the approximate β-Poisson model parameter α (R = 0.700, p < 0.001). Integrating this genotype-parameter mapping into the "airqmra" workflow enabled proof-of-concept α prediction for three atmospheric MAGs and uncertainty-based inhalation risk assessment for five target pathogens, with some annual risks exceeding 10. Overall, this genome-informed framework connects atmospheric microbial processes to human inhalation exposure pathways, providing an environmental-human component relevant to One Health and advancing bioaerosol risk assessment from static reference-strain assumptions toward genome-informed approaches.

title: Applications of Machine Learning-Assisted MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry in Clinical Bacterial Analysis: Research Progress and Clinical Translation
abstract: The integration of matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) with machine learning offers clinical microbiology laboratories a way to rapidly obtain information on antimicrobial resistance, typing, and molecular markers beyond routine species identification. However, translation from research to clinical practice remains constrained by three major bottlenecks: substantial heterogeneity in spectral acquisition and preprocessing, the decisive influence of validation design on the strength of evidence, and a systematic lack of workflow evaluation data in implementation studies. Available evidence indicates that culture duration, measurement mode, and cross-center or temporal changes can substantially affect model generalizability. Yet most studies still focus on internal discrimination, with insufficient evaluation of calibration reliability, automated output coverage, confirmatory testing burden, and time gained in reporting; few studies directly link model outputs to antimicrobial adjustment or infection-control actions. This review synthesizes advances across five dimensions: spectrum formation, clinical tasks, validation design, laboratory workflow integration, and postdeployment monitoring. Based on the hierarchy of validation evidence, we propose that the field is moving from feature-association discovery toward validation of clinical transferability. Future priorities should therefore shift from increasingly complex algorithms to standardized multicenter spectrum-sharing and validation frameworks and prospective workflow studies that determine whether additional spectral information can yield measurable time or resource savings.

title: Novel Pd(II) Rollover Complexes with Antimicrobial and Antibiofilm Activity
abstract: The escalating global crisis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) urgently demands the development of structurally diverse antimicrobial agents with novel mechanisms of action, including metal-based compounds. Herein, we report the synthesis and characterization of a series of palladium-(II) complexes incorporating the 2-(2'-pyridyl)-quinoline (pyqui) ligand. In addition to a simple N^N adduct [Pd-(pyqui)-(OAc)] (), rollover cyclometalation allowed the synthesis of less-common rollover-cyclometalated dimers [Pd-(pyqui-H)-(μ-OAc)]() and [Pd-(pyqui-H)-(μ-Cl)](), and mononuclear rollover derivatives [Pd-(pyqui-H)-(OAc)-(PPh)] () and [Pd-(pyqui-H)-(Cl)-(PPh)] (). The new compounds were comprehensively characterized by elemental analysis, FT-IR spectroscopy, and multinuclear (H,C,P) NMR spectroscopy, including two-dimensional experiments. Dynamic NMR studies revealed the coexistence of transoid and cisoid isomers in solution for the cyclometalated dimer. The antimicrobial and antibiofilm properties of the complexes were evaluated against clinically relevant Gram-positive bacteria (,), Gram-negative bacteria (,,), and the fungal pathogen, using agar well diffusion, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC), and minimum biofilm inhibitory concentration (MBIC) assays. The rollover mononuclear complexesandwere the most active compounds, exhibiting broad-spectrum antibacterial activity together with significant antibiofilm effects, particularly against Gram-positive pathogens.

title: Maternal group B Streptococcus colonization and antimicrobial susceptibility in an Inland region of Portugal: A five-year retrospective study
abstract: To determine the prevalence of maternal group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonization and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns in an inland region of Portugal, with particular emphasis on non-beta-lactam agents relevant to intrapartum prophylaxis. A retrospective laboratory-based observational study included eligible GBS screening episodes processed at the Local Health Unit of Guarda between 2019 and 2023. Demographic, sampling-site, healthcare-setting, and antimicrobial susceptibility data were analyzed. Resistance proportions were compared using Cochran's Q test, followed by exact McNemar tests with Holm correction. Among 2,457 eligible screening episodes, 378 were GBS-positive, corresponding to a prevalence of 15.4% (95% confidence interval: 14.0-16.9%). The median maternal age was 32 years (interquartile range: 28-36). Among 378 positive screening episodes, GBS was isolated from the vaginal specimen in 56 cases (14.8%) and from the rectal specimen in 95 (25.1%). Both vaginal and rectal specimens were positive in 227 cases (60.1%). Benzylpenicillin demonstrated preserved activity, with 343/346 isolates (99.1%) classified as susceptible or susceptible at increased exposure. Ceftriaxone susceptibility was observed in 72/76 isolates (94.7%), and all isolates tested for vancomycin were susceptible (347/347). Resistance was higher for erythromycin (104/286; 36.4%) and clindamycin (100/347; 28.8%). Concurrent resistance occurred in 33/257 isolates (12.8%). Resistance proportions differed significantly across the five agents (Cochran's Q(4) = 55.15; p < 0.001). Maternal GBS colonization remained frequent. Benzylpenicillin retained high in vitro activity, whereas substantial resistance to clindamycin and erythromycin reinforces the need for isolate-specific testing before clindamycin is selected for alternative intrapartum prophylaxis and supports continued regional surveillance.

title: High-risk detection of carbapenem-resistant and extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli in wild boar in Tunisia
abstract: This study aimed to assess the occurrence of antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli (E. coli) strains from fecal samples of hunted wild boar carcasses at both phenotypic and molecular levels. A total of 110 fecal samples were collected from hunted wild boar carcasses across five Tunisian governorates from October 2018 to December 2020. Several E. coli strains were recovered, and their antimicrobial susceptibility profiles, including extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) and carbapenemase production, were assessed. Molecular characterization was performed using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to identify phylogenetic groups, antimicrobial resistance genes, virulence genes, and integrons. A total of 55 E. coli strains were obtained, of which 52.7% were multidrug-resistant (MDR). The most frequently detected β-lactamase gene was bla(45.5%), followed by bla(30.9%) and bla(25.5%). Carbapenemase genes bla, blaand blawere identified in 6(10.9%), 3(5.5%) and 2(3.6%) strains, respectively. Plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance genes (qnrA, qnrS, qnrB and aac(6')-Ib-cr) and virulence-associated genes (fimH, traT, ibeA, fyuA, iutA, aer, stx-1, stx-2, cdt3, ehxA papGIII, eae and sfa/focDE) were variably detected. Class 1 and class 2 integron were found in 41.8% and 10.9% of the strains, respectively, and various gene cassettes were identified in class 1 integron, including aadA1, aac(6')-Ib-cr-aar-3, dfrA16, and VIM-28-Orf1-Orf2. This study revealed a high occurrence of multidrug-resistant E. coli exhibiting diverse virulence factors and genetic diversity linked to integrons in wild boars, underscoring their role as carriers of MDR pathogens. These findings raised a serious public health concern related to the potential risk of transmission of these strains among domestic the environment, and humans.

title: Reprogramming the Kyn-13 Locus of Daptomycin Unlocks a Serendipitous Theranostic Paradigm
abstract: Driven by the escalating multidrug-resistant superbug crisis (e.g., methicillin- and vancomycin-resistant strains) and the sparse clinical lipopeptide pipeline, we designed and synthesized 36 daptomycin derivatives, termed "kynurarylmycins", based on the facile regiospecific reductive amination approach at the Kyn-13 site of daptomycin with diverse aromatic aldehydes. Systematic SAR analysis revealed Kyn-13 arylation as a highly effective strategy to boost antibacterial potency. The lead candidateexhibits outstanding broad-spectrum activity against high-priority Gram-positive pathogens, including clinical isolates, outperforming daptomycin and vancomycin by 32- and 512-fold, respectively. Mechanistically,disrupts cell envelope activity via two independent pathways: it induces faster and stronger membrane depolarization with mild permeabilization to disrupt membrane homeostasis, and augments inhibition of cell wall biosynthesis. This dual-targeted lethality translates into superiortherapeutic efficacy in murine infection models. Serendipitously, this modification remodels daptomycin's intrinsic photophysics, triggering marked fluorescence turn-on in bacterial lipid microenvironments for high-contrast, wash-free, label-free live imaging. This work redefines Kyn-13 as a dual pharmacological and photophysical hub, offering an unprecedented theranostic paradigm for combating antimicrobial resistance.

title: Structural Basis for Recognition of a Gonococcal Lipooligosaccharide Epitope by Monoclonal Antibody 2C7 Informs Vaccine and Immunotherapeutic Design
abstract: , the causative agent of gonorrhea, represents an escalating global health concern because of the rapid spread of antimicrobial resistance and the continued lack of an effective vaccine. The lipooligosaccharide (LOS) epitope targeted by monoclonal antibody 2C7 is highly conserved and expressed by the majority of clinical isolates, highlighting its potential as an attractive target for therapeutic and vaccine-based interventions. To define the molecular basis for 2C7 recognition, we structurally characterized mAb 2C7 bound to an LOS-derived octasaccharide. NMR and a 1.6 Å crystal structure of the Fab 2C7-octasaccharide complex showed that mAb 2C7 recognizes the β- and γ-glycan chains through an extensive network of hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic interactions within the Fab binding cleft. MD simulations indicated that β and γ chains form stable, specific interactions with 2C7, whereas α-chain contacts are transient. Guided by structure, we synthesized a heptose II-linked β/γ-chain tetrasaccharide with its carrier-protein conjugate bound mAb 2C7 by ELISA and Western blotting. ITC revealed affinities comparable to the octasaccharide, confirming retention of key binding determinants. Binding was enthalpy-driven, consistent with crystallographic and MD-defined polar contacts. NMR confirmed engagement of all four residues, established as the minimal 2C7 epitope. These results provide a structural framework for the rational development of glycan-based vaccines and antibody therapeutics targeting antimicrobial-resistant.

title: Dipole moment governs antihypertensive drug-promoted plasmid conjugation in activated sludge independent of pharmacological action
abstract: Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are global hotspots for the plasmid-mediated horizontal transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Although antihypertensive drugs (AHDs) with diverse pharmacological modes of action (MOA) are ubiquitous in WWTPs, whether their effects on bacterial conjugation are MOA-dependent remains unclear. Here, we show that nine AHDs representing four distinct MOAs all significantly promote RP4 plasmid transfer between wastewater-isolated E. coli strains. Strikingly, the average hormetic zone for conjugative transfer (ΔA) does not correlate with pharmacological MOA but is instead strictly driven by the molecular dipole moment (μ) of the tested AHDs. This phenomenon is independent of AHD degradation kinetics and is mechanistically linked to bacterial biochemical responses, particularly increased intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and increased cell membrane permeability. Integrative mechanistic modelling further reveals that the promotion of conjugative transfer is fundamentally driven by a host-mediated cascade initiated by specific pollutant-protein interactions and the regulation of the key donor-cell genes ompT and ydjA, with a secondary contribution from recipient cells, rather than by direct modulation of RP4 plasmid gene expression. Moreover, AHDs exposure consistently exacerbate ARGs risk in activated sludge systems, and the overarching ARGs risk index (ARRI) remains tightly correlated with μ. Collectively, these findings redefine the molecular basis of AHD-driven ARG propagation, establishing μ as a key physicochemical determinant for ARG risk screening and mitigation in WWTPs, and support a shift away from MOA-centric environmental risk assessment of non-antibiotic pharmaceuticals.
